Appendix A Model Architecture: Additional Details

Expands Section 2.1. We collect here the implementation-level details of the predictor block: the channel-pair derivation behind factorised RoPE (Section A.1); the per-block view bias under grouped-query attention (Section A.2); the per-embodiment input projection (Section A.4); the embodiment-id breakdown that yields |ℰ|=26|\mathcal{E}|{=}26 (Section A.5); and the predictor scaling sweep across all eight scales used in the scaling law of Section 3 (Section A.6). All notation is shared with Section 2.1; in particular, ℓ\ell is reserved for the predictor layer index and τ\tau for autoregressive rollout steps.

Table 4 summarises how the RoboJEPA predictor differs from the action-conditioned V-JEPA 2 predictor (V-JEPA 2-AC) (Assran et al., 2025) it builds on. The two share the same backbone family and the same next-frame prediction parameterisation; RoboJEPA changes the normalisation, position encoding, and the conditioning that supports cross-view, cross-embodiment world modeling.

A.1 Factorised multi-axis RoPE

Each per-head channel space {0,…,dh−1}\{0,\dots,d_{h}-1\} partitions into four contiguous, equal-size sub-blocks of width dax=dh/4d_{\mathrm{ax}}{=}d_{h}/4, one per spatio-temporal axis. Fix the enumeration 𝒜max={t,i,j,v}\mathcal{A}_{\max}\!=\!\{t,i,j,v\} for the time, height, width, and view axes, and let jαj_{\alpha} denote the starting channel of axis α\alpha, so

{0,…,dh−1}=⨆α∈𝒜max{oα,oα+1,…,oα+dax−1},ot=0,oi=dax,oj=2dax,ov=3dax.\begin{gathered}\{0,\dots,d_{h}-1\}\;=\;\bigsqcup_{\alpha\in\mathcal{A}_{\max}}\big\{o_{\alpha},\,o_{\alpha}+1,\,\dots,\,o_{\alpha}+d_{\mathrm{ax}}-1\big\},\\ o_{t}=0,\;o_{i}=d_{\mathrm{ax}},\;o_{j}=2d_{\mathrm{ax}},\;o_{v}=3d_{\mathrm{ax}}.\end{gathered} (6)

Within axis α\alpha, the sub-block is partitioned in turn into dax/2d_{\mathrm{ax}}/2 channel pairs (oα+2​m,oα+2​m+1)\big(o_{\alpha}+2m,\,o_{\alpha}+2m+1\big) for m∈{0,…,dax/2−1}m\!\in\!\{0,\dots,d_{\mathrm{ax}}/2-1\}. We use the channel-pair index mm rather than the conventional kk to avoid collision with the key tensor kk. Each pair is rotated as a 2-D vector by the per-pair angle

θα(m)(p)=p⋅10000−2m/dax,p=posα∈ℕ\theta_{\alpha}^{(m)}(p)\;=\;p\cdot 10000^{-2m/d_{\mathrm{ax}}},\qquad p\;=\;\mathrm{pos}_{\alpha}\;\in\;\mathbb{N} (7)

evaluated at the integer coordinate of the token along axis α\alpha (time index for α=t\alpha\!=\!t, row for α=i\alpha\!=\!i, column for α=j\alpha\!=\!j, view slot for α=v\alpha\!=\!v); this matches the lang frequency convention used by the predictor’s RotaryEmbedding module (Su et al., 2024). Concretely, for a query channel pair (qoα+2​m,qoα+2​m+1)\big(q_{o_{\alpha}+2m},\,q_{o_{\alpha}+2m+1}\big) at axis position p=posαp\!=\!\mathrm{pos}_{\alpha},

(qoα+2​m′qoα+2​m+1′)=(cos⁡θα(m)​(p)−sin⁡θα(m)​(p)sin⁡θα(m)​(p)cos⁡θα(m)​(p))​(qoα+2​mqoα+2​m+1),\begin{pmatrix}q^{\prime}_{o_{\alpha}+2m}\\ q^{\prime}_{o_{\alpha}+2m+1}\end{pmatrix}\;=\;\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta_{\alpha}^{(m)}(p)&-\sin\theta_{\alpha}^{(m)}(p)\\ \sin\theta_{\alpha}^{(m)}(p)&\;\,\cos\theta_{\alpha}^{(m)}(p)\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}q_{o_{\alpha}+2m}\\ q_{o_{\alpha}+2m+1}\end{pmatrix}, (8)

and identically for the key channels. Pairs in different axis sub-blocks rotate independently and at independent frequencies, so the inner product ⟨q′,k′⟩\langle q^{\prime},k^{\prime}\rangle telescopes into a sum of per-axis, per-pair terms whose differences depend only on relative positions Δ​posα=posα−posα′\Delta\!\mathrm{pos}_{\alpha}=\mathrm{pos}_{\alpha}-\mathrm{pos}^{\prime}_{\alpha}. This relative-position property lets the predictor generalize across V∈{1,2}V\!\in\!\{1,2\} views and across the training and deployment patch grids of Section 2.2 without re-learning positional codes.

Under multi-view training (Vmax=2V_{\max}{=}2) we use the full 4-axis partition 𝒜={t,i,j,v}\mathcal{A}\!=\!\{t,i,j,v\}: the vv-axis sub-block contributes its own rotation, and viewpoint identity is additionally supplied by the per-block additive bias of Section A.2 (the two are complementary). For purely single-view runs (V=1V{=}1) the vv-axis sub-block carries no rotation and is left as the identity. Action and state tokens are detached from the visual slab before the RoPE rotation is applied: only the time component of RoPE rotates them (indexed by their step id), so that a single proprioceptive token per step does not spuriously inherit a spatial position.

A.2 Per-block view bias under grouped-query attention

The view information is encoded into the model in two ways. First, the view position encoding disambiguates different views of tokens with the same spatio-temporal position. This is achieved by rotating the view-axis sub-block (dh/4d_{h}/4 channels per head). However, the view position only informs the model that two different views are distinct without any encoding of the type of the content (e.g. the model has to know which view represents the side camera looking from the left and which one is mounted on the wrist). One way of dealing with it is to just let the model learn this end-to-end; however, we decided to directly inject the view information as a learnable bias added across the full head width of visual-token queries and keys after the four-axis RoPE rotation:

qℓ(v)←qℓ(v)+Uℓ​[c(v)],kℓ(v)←kℓ(v)+Uℓ​[c(v)],q_{\ell}^{(v)}\,\leftarrow\,q_{\ell}^{(v)}+U_{\ell}\!\big[c^{(v)}\big],\qquad k_{\ell}^{(v)}\,\leftarrow\,k_{\ell}^{(v)}+U_{\ell}\!\big[c^{(v)}\big], (9)

with Uℓ∈ℝ|𝒱|×dhU_{\ell}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|\times d_{h}} a learnable view embedding (zero-initialised), broadcast across all query and KV heads. This bias supplements, rather than replaces, the view-axis rotation. A learned global embodiment vector Eemb​[e]E_{\mathrm{emb}}[e] and a per-view embedding Eview​[c(v)]E_{\mathrm{view}}[c^{(v)}] are added once at the predictor input.

The strong-view conditioning of Equation 9 is a zero-initialised, layer-wise additive bias indexed by the semantic camera id c(v)∈𝒱c^{(v)}\!\in\!\mathcal{V} (left, right, wrist, front, back, head, top), implemented as Uℓ∈ℝ|𝒱|×dhU_{\ell}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|\times d_{h}} for each ℓ∈{1,…,Nlayers}\ell\!\in\!\{1,\dots,N_{\text{layers}}\} and added to all dhd_{h} channels of every visual token’s queries and keys after the RoPE rotation of Equation 8. Concretely, let Qℓ∈ℝN×hq×dhQ_{\ell}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{N\times h_{q}\times d_{h}} and Kℓ∈ℝN×hk​v×dhK_{\ell}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{N\times h_{kv}\times d_{h}} be the post-RoPE query and key tensors of layer ℓ\ell for a per-step token bag of length NN, and let bℓ(v):=Uℓ​[c(v)]∈ℝdhb_{\ell}^{(v)}\!:=\!U_{\ell}[c^{(v)}]\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{d_{h}} be the bias gathered for view vv. Under grouped-query attention (Ainslie et al., 2023) with hqh_{q} query heads and hk​vh_{kv} KV heads sharing the same head dimension dhd_{h}, the bias is added by the broadcast rule

Qℓ[n,r,:]+=bℓ(v⁡(n))∀r∈{1,…,hq},Kℓ[n,r,:]+=bℓ(v⁡(n))∀r∈{1,…,hk​v},Q_{\ell}[n,r,:]\;\mathrel{+}=\;b_{\ell}^{(v(n))}\quad\forall\,r\!\in\!\{1,\dots,h_{q}\},\qquad K_{\ell}[n,r,:]\;\mathrel{+}=\;b_{\ell}^{(v(n))}\quad\forall\,r\!\in\!\{1,\dots,h_{kv}\}, (10)

for every visual token index nn with view assignment v⁡(n)v(n); that is, the same dhd_{h}-vector bℓ(v)b_{\ell}^{(v)} is broadcast across all query heads and all KV heads of layer ℓ\ell, so the table UℓU_{\ell} has no head dimension and the parameter count is |𝒱|​dh|\mathcal{V}|\,d_{h} per layer (for the 1B model: 7⋅=8967\cdot 128\!=\!896 parameters per layer, 40⋅=35,84040\cdot 896\!=\!35{,}840 in total). The bias is not added to action or state tokens, since these have no view assignment; their post-RoPE queries and keys propagate through the attention block unchanged.

This per-layer additive bias supplements the vv-axis RoPE rotation of Equation 6: under our default strong-view configuration both signals are active, the rotation contributes a relative-view phase to attention scores, and the bias contributes a dhd_{h}-wide per-layer per-camera offset on top of it. The combination gives a stable handle on viewpoint identity for multi-view planning (Section 2.2); zero initialisation of UℓU_{\ell} makes loading a checkpoint trained without strong view conditioning a no-op at step 00.

A.3 Attention masking

We use a similar attention mask to V-JEPA 2-AC (Assran et al., 2025) but extend it to multiple views: attention is timestep-level causal and restricted to a local temporal window of 88 timesteps, while within a step all V​Hp​WpVH_{p}W_{p} visual tokens (plus the action and state tokens) attend omnidirectionally (any-to-any). More precisely, the rasterized sequence of tokens has T×NtokT\times N_{\text{tok}} tokens in total and the token at index kk can attend to tokens with indices jj such that ⌊kNtok⌋−7⩽⌊jNtok⌋⩽⌊kNtok⌋\lfloor\frac{k}{N_{\text{tok}}}\rfloor-7\leqslant\lfloor\frac{j}{N_{\text{tok}}}\rfloor\leqslant\lfloor\frac{k}{N_{\text{tok}}}\rfloor. Schematically, this means that packing the sequence as TT frame-blocks of size NtokN_{\mathrm{tok}} given by Equation 20, the attention mask between blocks is banded lower-triangular: each block of size Ntok×NtokN_{\mathrm{tok}}{\times}N_{\mathrm{tok}} is fully attended within the diagonal band of width WtW_{t} and zero outside it. This trick makes the computational cost of attention grow linearly as a function of the step number and it alleviates the problem of the position extrapolation – the predicted content quality depends only on the accumulated error, not the ability of the model to extrapolate, because it never observes a sequence longer than the window size. This is a classical trick for language models and world models (Assran et al., 2025; Po et al., 2025; PAN Team et al., 2025). The bounded window keeps the per-step computational cost of attention constant and makes the predictor KV-cacheable in 𝒪⁡(Wt⋅V⋅Hp⋅Wp)\mathcal{O}(W_{t}\cdot V\cdot H_{p}\cdot W_{p}) keys per layer; Section 2.2 uses this at deployment.

A.4 Per-embodiment input projection

Every embodiment ee owns its own input weight matrix Wa(e)W_{a}^{(e)} in a single multi-embodiment linear projection. The raw action vector at∈ℝdaa_{t}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{d_{a}} is zero-padded to a common width damaxd_{a}^{\max} jointly large enough to absorb the widest action convention in our mixture (Section 2.2; for the 1B run damax=dsmax=64d_{a}^{\max}{=}d_{s}^{\max}{=}64, set by the chunked DROID joint_vel action-key variant which produces an ⋅=648\!\cdot\!8\!=\!64-D mega-action) before projection,

a~t=[at; 0damax−da]∈ℝdamax,ActTok⁡(at,e)=(Wa(e))⊤​a~t+ba(e)+PEta,\tilde{a}_{t}\;=\;\big[\,a_{t}\,;\,\bm{0}_{d_{a}^{\max}-d_{a}}\,\big]\;\in\;\mathbb{R}^{d_{a}^{\max}},\qquad\mathrm{ActTok}(a_{t},e)\;=\;(W_{a}^{(e)})^{\!\top}\,\tilde{a}_{t}\,+\,b_{a}^{(e)}\,+\,\mathrm{PE}_{t}^{a}, (11)

with Wa(e)∈ℝdamax×DW_{a}^{(e)}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{d_{a}^{\max}\times D}, and an analogous projection StTok⁡(st,e)\mathrm{StTok}(s_{t},e) for state; PEt{a,s}\mathrm{PE}_{t}^{\{a,s\}} are 1-D sin–cos positional embeddings over time. This lets a single predictor consume the heterogeneous action / state conventions of Section 2.2 (chunked DROID controller commands, multi-D AgiBot World dual-arm states, planar Language-Table poses, etc.) without per-embodiment branching at the transformer level: the embodiment identity affects only the input projection.

The action token participates in self-attention as a regular token: the projected vector ActTok⁡(at,e)\mathrm{ActTok}(a_{t},e) is concatenated to the per-step token bag and attends to (and is attended by) all visual and state tokens of the same step, and all visual / action / state tokens within the local temporal window WtW_{t}. The state token participates symmetrically. Token-style conditioning, in contrast to additive action embedding, lets the predictor express step-dependent gating of action effects (e.g., the gripper acting differently early vs. late in a grasp) without inflating the per-step input dimensionality.

A.5 Robot-id breakdown

The training mixture spans 1212 physical robotic platforms (the Total row of Table 1). We treat each (platform, action-source) pair as a distinct robot id, which yields |ℰ|=26|\mathcal{E}|{=}26 ids, split into 1212 default state-delta ids (one per platform) plus 1414 extra splits for those datasets that ship more than one synchronized controller stream or distinct state convention not collapsed by the action-key pipeline of Section B.7. Table 5 lists the visible breakdown (#\# / Platform / Notes); the internal embodiment_name strings used by the training config are collected in the table footnote.

A.6 Predictor scaling sweep

For the scaling study of Section 3, we train 2222M, 5050M, 100100M, 300300M, 11B, 22B, 44B, and 88B variants with the same block recipe (pre-norm GQA + GELU MLP, factorised 4-axis RoPE on (t,i,j,v)(t,i,j,v) supplemented by the per-block view bias of Equation 9, encoder, padded action / state widths, local temporal window, optimizer schedule). The eight variants differ only in NlayersN_{\text{layers}}, DD, and the GQA head counts (hq,hk​v)(h_{q},\,h_{kv}) (Table 6); the head dimension dh=128d_{h}{=}128 and the MLP hidden ratio 4​D4D are held constant. The KV head count matches the query head count at the smallest scales and approaches hk​v=hq/2h_{kv}=h_{q}/2 as model size increases.

Appendix B Data: Additional Details

Expands Section 2.2. Heterogeneous robot data become a single token stream by being normalized onto a common temporal grid (Section B.6), a common padded action / state width (Section B.7), and a common semantic camera vocabulary (Section B.9). The on-disk format (Section B.3) and the non-trivial per-dataset conversions needed to reach it (Section B.4) make this routing reproducible, the view-mixed-rank mixture (Section B.5) fixes the sampling, and the full per-dataset breakdown lives in Section B.2.

B.1 Dataset mixture and unification

Actions.

For most datasets, the per-step action is the difference between consecutive states (which we refer to as the state-delta action): whether it is an end-effector (EEF) absolute pose, absolute joint angles, a commanded motion, or any combination of those for multiarm or wheeled robots. The same demonstration can often be described through several such parameterisations at once (for example joint angle control or EEF pose control), and each one shows the world model the same behavior from a different control perspective, acting as an action-level augmentation. We exploit this: we found it beneficial to train on different action parameterisations of the same embodiment whenever they are available. For example, with the DROID dataset arm we cannot only train on state-delta of the end-effector but also on the velocities of the end-effector or joint angles. Early in the work, we found that this improves the world model at a fixed training compute budget.

In addition to that, different embodiments provide a much richer potential learning signal for world models since they expose manipulation through different action spaces, each following its own unique dynamics and a set of constraints. Therefore, the world model has more potential to learn the underlying physics and dynamics of the world than with one embodiment. We treat each (platform, action-space) pair as a distinct embodiment id, giving |ℰ|=26|\mathcal{E}|{=}26 over the 1212 physical platforms (26=1226=12 default state-delta ids +14+14 extra splits; full enumeration in Table 5).

We use a lean per-embodiment linear projection of actions to facilitate learning a shared latent action tokenization within the world model. The dimensionality of the actions also varies. For the single-arm end-effector delta poses, we use seven dimensions that represent a 66D translation+rotation and gripper closure. For dual arm platforms (e.g. AgileX in RoboMind or AgiBot World), this gets doubled since we have to control two arms independently. For wheeled platforms, the action space is extended by the commanded actions for the wheeled navigation - for example the RoboCasa platform reserves four actions for navigation atop the standard 77D EEF control and 1X reserves 22D for navigation (see more details in Tables 7 and B.7).

Unification and sampling.

To facilitate efficient training, we convert all datasets into the unified data format. Since datasets are collected with different sensor frequencies, loading continuous chunks of data would often lead to an overly short horizon for prediction. Additionally, different datasets have different motion velocities due to differences in data collection mechnisms – often different teleoperated platforms scale human motion to a faster or slower motion of the robot. Therefore, we employ different frame sampling frequencies for different datasets which we report in Table 7 (see Section B.6 for details). Each frame is processed via the image embedding of the V-JEPA 2.1 recipe (Mur-Labadia et al., 2026), whose features performed strongly in policy-based evaluations of latent diffusion world models (Nilaksh et al., 2026) on Bridge V2 (Walke et al., 2023). To correctly represent the total action between sampled frames, we either use the total measured state delta action or the concatenated chunk of commanded actions between sampled frames when working with commanded actions. The world model does not have a well-defined notion of modeling frequency. Instead, we simply let the world model integrate the total motion represented by the action into the next predicted latent state.

B.2 Per-dataset breakdown

Table 1 collapses the OXE, AgiBot World, and RoboMind sub-corpora into single rows. Table 7 gives the full per-dataset breakdown with resolutions and source FPS.

B.3 Standardised on-disk format

Every source dataset is re-packaged into a single object-storage layout so that the dataloader does not need per-source branching beyond a thin adapter that emits the standard tuple consumed by the predictor. Each trajectory exposes three groups: an MP4-encoded camera stream per view (cameras/), HDF5 datasets holding the native proprioceptive vector (trajectory/observation/robot_state/), and, when the source ships a controller stream, raw controller commands (trajectory/action/). Episode-level metadata (e.g. DROID building/labs fields used by the negative filter that drops setup-room recordings) is recorded in a per-dataset aggregated_metadata.json; a per-dataset index maps episode ids to S3 paths, episode lengths, and per-camera availability so the sampler operates on this index without touching object storage. Per-clip sampling reads T=16T{=}16 frames at the world-model rate (Section B.6) and VV cameras (Section B.9); intrinsics, extrinsics, and uncalibrated metadata are loaded as NaN-filled placeholders and discarded by the predictor in this configuration.

B.4 Per-dataset postprocessing

Beyond the common repackaging of Section B.3, several datasets require non-trivial numerical, geometric, or video conversions before they can enter the shared token stream. We describe these here grouped by the kind of transformation; the trivial relabelling of fields onto the common schema is omitted.

Video decoding and re-encoding.

Every source is emitted as one MP4 per view at its native frame rate (Table 7). Most OXE (Open X-Embodiment Collaboration et al., 2023) sources ship RLDS/TFDS records with per-step RGB arrays, which we re-encode to MP4 (e.g. 11 fps for RoboNet (Dasari et al., 2019), 55 fps for Bridge (Ebert et al., 2022)/MT-Opt (Kalashnikov et al., 2021)/Language-Table (Lynch et al., 2023), 1010 fps for RT-1 (Brohan et al., 2023)/QT-Opt (Kalashnikov et al., 2018)/BC-Z (Jang et al., 2022)/FMB (Luo et al., 2024)). RoboMind (Wu et al., 2024b) stores each frame as a JPEG byte-string inside HDF5: we decode every frame individually, falling back to a raw-buffer reshape (720×1280720{\times}1280 or 480×640480{\times}640) when the JPEG header is missing, and correct the channel order from BGR to RGB for the real Franka streams (the simulated streams are already RGB). For DROID (Khazatsky et al., 2024) we discard the stereo/SVO recordings and keep the rectified monocular left, right, and wrist MP4 streams. For sources with multiple nominal cameras we detect and drop all-zero (absent) camera streams so they are not written as empty views (e.g. the unused auxiliary cameras in Bridge V2 (Walke et al., 2023)).

Forward kinematics for joint-only sources.

Roboset (Bharadhwaj et al., 2024) and LeRobot (Cadene et al., 2024) record only joint encoders, with no end-effector pose. We reconstruct the end-effector Cartesian pose with a differentiable forward-kinematics model of the corresponding arm (a Franka Panda for Roboset, the SO-101 URDF for LeRobot), applied to both the state trajectory and, for Roboset, the commanded-joint trajectory to recover a Cartesian action. LeRobot joint encoders are first converted from degrees to radians. For Roboset we additionally apply constant per-joint offsets (a +π/2+\pi/2 shift on the wrist joints of both state and action, and a −π/2-\pi/2 shift on one action joint) so that the joint zero convention matches the URDF used by the kinematics model.

Orientation representation.

Sources that store the end-effector orientation as a quaternion (RT-1, QT-Opt, MT-Opt, FMB, the simulated RoboMind Franka split) and the forward-kinematics outputs above are all converted to an x​y​zxyz Euler parameterisation, so that the entire mixture shares a single 33-D translation ++ 33-D Euler orientation convention for end-effector poses.

Gripper normalisation.

Gripper signals are placed on a common [0,1][0,1] closedness scale. Roboset state grippers are divided by their observed open width (0.83050.8305) and clipped to [0,1][0,1], and its command grippers are affinely mapped from [−1,1][-1,1] to [0,1][0,1]. WidowX sources (Bridge and Bridge V2) invert and clip the raw gripper signal, g←1−clip⁡(g,0,1)g\leftarrow 1-\mathrm{clip}(g,0,1), so that larger values consistently denote a more closed gripper.

Multi-arm and humanoid assembly.

Bimanual and humanoid embodiments are assembled into a single per-step vector. For the RoboMind AgileX dual-arm platform we concatenate the left and right end-effector poses and the left and right arm joints, taking each arm’s last joint as its gripper. Bridge (v1) actions, which are stored as separate translation and rotation-delta fields, are concatenated into a single delta-pose action vector, and BC-Z end-effector poses are assembled from separately stored translation and axis-angle observations.

B.5 View-mixed-rank training: mixture composition

The 1B run uses Wddp=256W_{\mathrm{ddp}}{=}256 data-parallel ranks (32 nodes ×\times 8 H100s), partitioned into two equally sized view-groups:

  • •

    Two-view group (ranks 0​…​1270{\dots}127): each rank loads Vg=2V_{g}{=}2 camera views per clip with Bg=2B_{g}{=}2 clips per microbatch and gradient accumulation Kg=1K_{g}{=}1, contributing 44 view-clips per rank per step, i.e. 512512 view-clips group-wide.

  • •

    One-view group (ranks 128​…​255128{\dots}255): each rank loads Vg=1V_{g}{=}1 view per clip with Bg=2B_{g}{=}2, Kg=1K_{g}{=}1, contributing 22 view-clips per rank per step, i.e. 256256 view-clips group-wide.

This yields the effective per-step batch of 768768 view-clips (512512 clips) derived in Section C.1 (Equation 13). The two groups share predictor parameters and step the optimizer in lockstep.

Table 8 lists the per-(dataset, action-source) sampling weights for both groups in a single table, together with the per-row total. The top block lists datasets that ship two reliably informative external cameras and feed both groups; the lower block lists single-camera sources that feed only the 1-view group. For datasets appearing in both groups, the 1-view rank uses a contracted camera regex selected so that the rank still sees a representative external view (e.g. left/right exterior for DROID excludes the wrist; AgiBot World Robotiq is restricted to its head-mounted RGB stream).

Effective per-step mixture.

At the clip level the split is 50/5050/50; at the token-with-loss level the run sees 23\tfrac{2}{3} of the signal at V=2V{=}2 (the V=2V{=}2 clips contribute two view-clips each). Both view counts therefore appear in every optimizer step, so the per-block view conditioning (Equation 9) and the factorised RoPE of Section 2.1 are jointly exposed to both regimes rather than separated by curriculum.

B.6 Frame rate, decimation and the per-frame mask

Every dataset is normalized to a target world-model rate fwmf_{\text{wm}} that determines the temporal stride between consecutive frames in a clip. Source FPS varies by two orders of magnitude across the mixture (Table 7): 11 Hz for OXE RoboNet, 55–1010 Hz for most OXE sources, 2020–3030 Hz for RoboCasa / RoboMind / AgiBot / LeRobot, 6060 Hz for DROID. The loader decimates by the integer factor c=⌈fraw/fwm⌉c\;=\;\lceil f_{\text{raw}}/f_{\text{wm}}\rceil and indexes frames as np.arange(start_frame, end_frame, c), so one predictor step always corresponds to a fixed 1/fwm1/f_{\text{wm}} of robot wall-clock regardless of source FPS. Trajectories whose effective length falls below T=16T{=}16 are right-padded with zero frames, and a per-frame mask

mt,v= 1​[frame ​(t,v)​ is a real, non-padded sample]∈{0,1}m_{t,v}\;=\;\mathbb{1}[\text{frame }(t,v)\text{ is a real, non-padded sample}]\;\in\;\{0,1\} (12)

is propagated to the loss — the same mt,vm_{t,v} that gates the masked ℓ1\ell_{1} in Equation 5 and the rollout objective in Section 2.2. Within a single clip the mask is the same across views, mt,v≡mtm_{t,v}\!\equiv\!m_{t}, because clip-level padding is applied symmetrically to all VV streams; we keep the per-view subscript in Equation 5 for notational consistency with the V=1V{=}1 vs V=2V{=}2 rank groups.

Rate bridge fwm→fctrlf_{\text{wm}}\!\to\!f_{\text{ctrl}} at deployment.

At deployment the Franka controller of Section 2.2 runs at fctrl=10f_{\text{ctrl}}{=}10 Hz while the world model operates at fwm=5f_{\text{wm}}{=}5 Hz. The planner replans on every other controller tick and the 77-D end-effector delta returned by the planner is split into fctrl/fwm=2f_{\text{ctrl}}/f_{\text{wm}}{=}2 equal sub-steps emitted back-to-back; this keeps training and deployment aligned on the same 200200 ms predictor stride and isolates the controller from the world-model rate.

B.7 Action conditioning details

The mixture exposes two complementary action-vector pipelines per (dataset, action-source) pair. Each pair is a distinct embodiment id from the |ℰ|=26|\mathcal{E}|{=}26 registry consumed by the predictor’s per-embodiment input projection (Section 2.1); duplicates of the same physical platform under different action sources (e.g. the six DROID embodiments listed in Table 8) share encoder inputs but learn distinct Wa(e)W_{a}^{(e)}, Ws(e)W_{s}^{(e)} slices.

State-delta pipeline (default).

For most datasets the per-step action is computed as a finite difference of the synchronized state trajectory: Δ​xt∈ℝ3\Delta x_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{3} for the end-effector position, Δ​Rt∈𝔰​𝔬​(3)\Delta R_{t}\in\mathfrak{so}(3) for orientation (computed in the Lie algebra so that the magnitude is independent of the rotation representation used by the source), and a scalar Δ​gt\Delta g_{t} for the gripper. The vector concatenates these into a per-platform native width: 77-D for the standard Franka / Bridge / Kuka end-effector, 1414-D for AgileX (two end-effectors), 2323-D for AgiBot dual-arm, 2525-D for the 1X humanoid, and so on across the mixture.

Action-key pipeline (high-rate sources).

For datasets that ship a high-rate controller stream — DROID (four cartesian / joint, position / velocity variants) and RoboCasa (cartesian-position) — the loader instead reads the raw controller stream at frawf_{\text{raw}} and concatenates the fraw/fwmf_{\text{raw}}/f_{\text{wm}} sub-step commands within one world-model step into a single per-step vector. For DROID at →7.560\!\to\!7.5 Hz this yields a chunk of 88 controller commands per predictor step (up to 8×8=648{\times}8{=}64 dimensions); for RoboCasa at →520\!\to\!5 Hz it yields a chunk of 44 commands. This recovers the high-frequency controller signal (which the world model must match if its rollout is to drive a downstream planner — Section 2.2) without changing the fwmf_{\text{wm}} stride at which video features are produced.

Padding to damax=64d_{a}^{\max}{=}64 and per-embodiment projection.

To batch heterogeneous embodiments together within a single rank’s microbatch, every per-step action vector — whether a single state-delta or an action-key chunk — is right-zero-padded to the fixed width damax=64d_{a}^{\max}{=}64 used by the predictor’s per-embodiment input projection. The width 6464 is chosen jointly to absorb the widest native state-delta (the 2525-D 1X humanoid) and the largest action-key chunk emitted by the pipeline above. The per-embodiment projection Wa(e)∈ℝD×damaxW_{a}^{(e)}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{D\times d_{a}^{\max}} is a multi-embodiment linear (a single |ℰ|×D×damax|\mathcal{E}|\!\times\!D\!\times\!d_{a}^{\max} weight tensor indexed by embodiment id) that recovers the native action space from the padded slot. The same construction is mirrored on the proprioceptive side (dsmaxd_{s}^{\max}, Ws(e)W_{s}^{(e)}); the action and state tokens enter the predictor as na=ns=1n_{a}{=}n_{s}{=}1 tokens per step in Equation 20.

At deployment the planner of Section 2.2 targets a single Franka-style 77-D end-effector delta convention, so the action dimensionality the user sees on a real robot is fixed regardless of which subset of the mixture trained the model. The deployment pipeline mirrors the training-time padding and embodiment-id lookup exactly, so the projection Wa(e)W_{a}^{(e)} used at planning time is the same one trained against the corresponding state-delta variant.

B.8 Image preprocessing

The video tensor returned by the loader has shape [C,V,T,Himg,Wimg][C,V,T,H_{\text{img}},W_{\text{img}}] with C=3C{=}3, V∈{1,2}V\!\in\!\{1,2\} and T=16T{=}16 frames at fwmf_{\text{wm}}. Spatial cropping follows the V-JEPA 2.1 input recipe (Mur-Labadia et al., 2026): at training time each clip is randomly resized with aspect ratio sampled from [1.333,1.777][1.333,1.777] and area scale sampled from [0.5,1.0][0.5,1.0], then center-cropped to 240×320240{\times}320, while at evaluation we use a deterministic 1.0/1.01.0/1.0-scale crop of the same size. Random horizontal flips, auto-augmentation, motion shift and random erasing are disabled to avoid distorting end-effector geometry. Frames are normalized with the standard ImageNet statistics (Deng et al., 2009) expected by the V-JEPA 2.1 encoder (Mur-Labadia et al., 2026), and the resulting 240×320240{\times}320 tensor is fed to the frozen encoder which produces an Hp×Wp=15×20H_{p}{\times}W_{p}{=}15{\times}20 patch grid with De=1664D_{e}{=}1664 channels per patch.

B.9 Per-camera enumeration

Every physical camera in the mixture is mapped at load time to one of |𝒱|=7|\mathcal{V}|{=}7 semantic camera ids by a per-dataset regex map. Cameras with the same semantic role (e.g. all left-exterior cameras across DROID, Roboset, RoboMind, RoboCasa, OXE FMB) are mapped to the same id and therefore share the learned per-block view bias of Equation 9 regardless of which dataset they come from or whether the rank is V=1V{=}1 or V=2V{=}2. Table 9 reports the mapping in transposed form (semantic ids run across columns, datasets down rows).

Appendix C Training: Additional Details

Expands Section 2.2. We document the per-rank batch decomposition across view-groups (Section C.1). The loss is defined once in Equation 5.

We use data parallelism for models up to 22B parameters and FSDP2 for the 44B and 88B models during pretraining and short-horizon prediction training. For long-horizon prediction finetuning, we instead use data parallelism combined with tensor parallelism (tp=2\mathrm{tp}{=}2) for the 44B and 88B models. Sharing each sequence across two tensor-parallel GPUs allows an effective per-GPU batch size below one sequence in the most memory-intensive group (two-view, high-resolution), accommodating the K=10K{=}10 autoregressive rollout used during this cooldown.

C.1 Per-rank batch decomposition and view groups

The dataloader of Section 2.2 partitions the Wddp=256W_{\mathrm{ddp}}{=}256 DDP ranks into Gv=2G_{v}{=}2 view-groups, indexed by g∈{1,2}g\!\in\!\{1,2\}. Group gg owns Rg=128R_{g}{=}128 ranks, processes clips with VgV_{g} cameras (V1=1V_{1}{=}1, V2=2V_{2}{=}2), and runs KgK_{g} gradient-accumulation microbatches per optimizer step (K1=K2=1K_{1}{=}K_{2}{=}1 for the 1B run, but the same code path supports Kg>1K_{g}{>}1 on memory-constrained configurations). Each microbatch on a rank in group gg contains BgB_{g} clips (B2=2B_{2}{=}2 for g=2g{=}2, B1=2B_{1}{=}2 for g=1g{=}1). The effective number of clip-views consumed per optimizer step is therefore

Ncveff=∑g=1GvRg⋅Kg⋅Bg⋅Vg=⋅⋅⋅1+⋅⋅⋅2= 768,N_{\mathrm{cv}}^{\mathrm{eff}}\;=\;\sum_{g=1}^{G_{v}}R_{g}\cdot K_{g}\cdot B_{g}\cdot V_{g}\;=\;128\!\cdot\!1\!\cdot\!2\!\cdot\!1\;+\;128\!\cdot\!1\!\cdot\!2\!\cdot\!2\;=\;768, (13)

i.e. 256256 single-view clips and 256256 two-view clips (512512 clips, 768768 clip-views) per optimizer step. Because the encoder is run per-view independently, the encoder forward sees the full 768768 clip-views; the predictor processes each clip as a single sequence of T⋅(Vg​Hp​Wp+na+ns)T\!\cdot\!(V_{g}H_{p}W_{p}+n_{a}+n_{s}) tokens (concretely 16⋅30216\cdot 302 for g=1g{=}1 and 16⋅60216\cdot 602 for g=2g{=}2 with the geometry of Table 6).

C.2 Cooldown phase

The schedule of Section 2.2 is warmup–stable–decay (WSD) (Hu et al., 2024): warmup linear →η0\!\to\!\eta, then a long stable phase held flat at η=5×10−5\eta{=}5{\times}10^{-5}, then a cooldown (decay) phase. We do not run cooldown inline; instead we resume the final stable-phase checkpoint as a fresh job that (i) swaps the optimizer schedulers to a linear LR cooldown paired with a constant weight-decay schedule, (ii) raises the autoregressive rollout horizon from Kar=2K_{\mathrm{ar}}{=}2 to Kar=10K_{\mathrm{ar}}{=}10, and (iii) re-partitions the ranks into four view×\timesresolution groups. The LR decays as ηt=η⁡(1−min⁡(t,Ncool)/Ncool)\eta_{t}=\eta\,(1-\min(t,N_{\mathrm{cool}})/N_{\mathrm{cool}}) with Ncool=5000N_{\mathrm{cool}}{=}5000 optimizer steps, reaching 00 at the end; weight decay stays at 0.10.1 throughout (the cooldown is a pure LR sweep), and the per-group μ\muP lr_scale factors are preserved.

Four view×\timesresolution groups.

During cooldown the two view-groups of Section C.1 are each split by input resolution, giving four groups that evenly partition the world (25%25\% of ranks each on the 128128-rank 1B cooldown): two-view 240×320240{\times}320, two-view 480×640480{\times}640, one-view 240×320240{\times}320, and one-view 480×640480{\times}640. The predictor and the frozen V-JEPA 2.1 encoder are unchanged: at 480×640480{\times}640 the encoder’s 16×1616{\times}16 patching yields a 30×4030{\times}40 grid, i.e. Hp​Wp=1200H_{p}W_{p}{=}1200 tokens per view per frame versus 300300 at 240×320240{\times}320 (a 4×4\times increase), and the predictor’s factorised RoPE (Section A.1) interpolates to the larger grid with no new parameters. High-resolution groups use a smaller per-rank batch and matched gradient accumulation to keep per-GPU memory within budget; the gradient-synchronization machinery is unchanged, now aggregating four groups instead of two in the single per-step all-reduce.

C.3 Training hyperparameters

Table 10 lists the loss, optimizer, and cooldown settings for the 11B predictor, complementing the model configurations in Table 6.

C.4 DROID 3-view Finetuning at 720×\times1280

We additionally finetune a high-resolution DROID world model. It initializes from the 88B long-horizon prediction training checkpoint at 300,000300{,}000 pretraining steps (Section J.3), and the only things we change relative to the scaling runs are the input resolution and the number of views. Training uses DROID (Khazatsky et al., 2024) only, with three fixed views at 720×1280720{\times}1280 resolution over 1616 timesteps. The three views are the exterior-left, exterior-right, and wrist cameras, selected in this fixed order; this is unlike pretraining, where the views are sampled in a random order. With patch size 1616, each 720×1280720{\times}1280 view becomes a 45×80=3,60045{\times}80{=}3{,}600-token grid, so a full sequence is about 170,000170{,}000 input tokens. At this resolution the model would also generate more than 10,00010{,}000 tokens per forward pass, which highlights the utility of a feedforward world model that predicts all next-frame tokens in one pass.

We keep the same world-model objective as in pretraining but with a K=10K{=}10-step autoregressive rollout. We train for 2,0002{,}000 optimizer steps on 256256 GPUs (tensor-parallel tp=4\mathrm{tp}{=}4, giving 6464 data-parallel replicas and a global batch of 6464 sequences) with AdamW (weight decay 0.10.1, gradient clipping), warming the learning rate up to 5×10−55{\times}10^{-5} over 140140 optimization steps and then decaying it with a cosine schedule over the remaining steps. The per-step compute of this stage is the finetune row of Table 20.

Appendix D Diffusion Decoder: Additional Details

Expands Section 2.3.

Role and rate hierarchy.

The world model produces dense V-JEPA features at fwm=5f_{\mathrm{wm}}{=}5 Hz, i.e. one feature frame for every fourth RGB frame; the Cosmos tokenizer compresses the raw video time axis by 4×4{\times}, so each Cosmos latent frame aligns with exactly one V-JEPA frame. The decoder therefore does two jobs at once — reconstruct the appearance the V-JEPA features already encode, and imagine the three RGB frames of motion between consecutive V-JEPA frames. Because fwmf_{\mathrm{wm}} is low, the inter-frame motion the decoder needs to fabricate is small, which is why a relatively small DiT (∼800{\sim}800M parameters) suffices for 240×320240{\times}320 video.

Visualisation-only.

The decoder DϕD_{\phi} is used only for visualization: it is never invoked inside CEM, and no gradient flows between it and the world model. Its training data is exclusively frozen V-JEPA 2.1 encoder features (Mur-Labadia et al., 2026); the encoder, the predictor of Section 2.1, and both halves of the Cosmos-0.1-Tokenizer-CV4x8x8 (NVIDIA, 2025) are all frozen, and the only trainable parameters are those of DϕD_{\phi} itself.

Frame alignment between V-JEPA and Cosmos.

Throughout this appendix a decoder clip spans TdecT_{\text{dec}} V-JEPA steps (Tdec=8T_{\text{dec}}{=}8 in our experiments) and ν∈{0,…,Tdec}\nu\!\in\!\{0,\dots,T_{\text{dec}}\} indexes its frames (we reserve the symbol ff for the frozen V-JEPA encoder). To keep the two grids exactly aligned, the dataloader loads video at two frame rates simultaneously: a high-fps stream of 4​Tdec+14T_{\text{dec}}{+}1 RGB frames that the Cosmos encoder compresses into the latents to be denoised, and a low-fps stream of every fourth frame, i.e. the Tdec+1T_{\text{dec}}{+}1 RGB frames 0,4,…,4​Tdec0,4,\dots,4T_{\text{dec}}, that the V-JEPA encoder turns into conditioning features. Because the Cosmos tokenizer downsamples space by 8×8\times and time by 4×4\times, encoding the first frame on its own, the 4​Tdec+14T_{\text{dec}}{+}1 RGB frames yield Tdec+1T_{\text{dec}}{+}1 Cosmos latent frames of shape Hp×WpH_{p}{\times}W_{p} with 16 latent channels. The frame-rate multiplier equals the tokenizer’s 4×4{\times} temporal compression, so each Cosmos latent frame ν\nu corresponds to exactly one V-JEPA frame zνz_{\nu}; for Tdec=8T_{\text{dec}}{=}8 the clip has 99 V-JEPA frames (RGB frames 0,4,…,320,4,\dots,32), 3333 RGB frames and 99 Cosmos latent frames. Operating in this 8×8×48{\times}8{\times}4-compressed latent space, rather than on pixels, is what makes training a transformer denoiser on 240×320240{\times}320 video tractable on a single node.

DiT denoiser architecture.

DϕD_{\phi} is a PixArt-style diffusion transformer (Peebles and Xie, 2023; Chen et al., 2024b) with L=32L{=}32 blocks of hidden dimension d=1280d{=}1280. Each block uses grouped-query attention (Ainslie et al., 2023) with 2020 query heads and 1010 KV heads, an MLP ratio of 4.04.0, and rotary position embeddings (Su et al., 2024) on the attention queries and keys. Self-attention is restricted to a local temporal window of Wτ=4W_{\tau}{=}4 Cosmos frames (full attention across the spatial Hp×WpH_{p}{\times}W_{p} grid), which keeps the computational cost per token linear in the clip length and admits an efficient block-sparse mask while encouraging local temporal coherence. This Wτ=4W_{\tau}{=}4 window acts on Cosmos latents (themselves 4×4{\times} temporally compressed) and is distinct from the predictor’s Wt=8W_{t}{=}8-V-JEPA-frame window of Section 2.1.

Conditioning.

The V-JEPA features z0:Tdecz_{0:T_{\text{dec}}} enter DϕD_{\phi} through dense spatial concat conditioning. The features are upsampled with nearest-neighbour interpolation to the Cosmos grid (in space; in time the two grids already match one-to-one) and concatenated, along the channel axis, with the patchified noisy Cosmos input; a learned linear Linear⁡(d+1664)→d\mathrm{Linear}(d{+}1664)\!\to\!d then mixes the two streams into the input token embeddings of the first DiT block. The adaLN modulation (Peebles and Xie, 2023) of every DiT block is conditioned only on the diffusion noise level: for each Cosmos frame ν\nu, the embedding of its timestep tνt_{\nu} produces six per-block parameters (shiftattn,scaleattn,gateattn,shiftffn,scaleffn,gateffn)(\text{shift}_{\text{attn}},\text{scale}_{\text{attn}},\text{gate}_{\text{attn}},\text{shift}_{\text{ffn}},\text{scale}_{\text{ffn}},\text{gate}_{\text{ffn}}) that modulate both the attention and FFN sub-layers for that frame. Concretely, with input tokens h∈ℝB×T×N×dh\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times T\times N\times d},

h′=gate⊙Sublayer​(LN​(h)⊙(1+scale)+shift)+h,h^{\prime}\;=\;\text{gate}\,\odot\,\text{Sublayer}\!\big(\text{LN}(h)\odot(1{+}\text{scale})+\text{shift}\big)\;+\;h, (14)

applied per Cosmos frame before flattening back to the joint (T⋅N)(T\!\cdot\!N)-token sequence consumed by attention.

Training objective.

We train DϕD_{\phi} with a standard DDPM (Ho et al., 2020) forward process applied to the Cosmos latents. Let tν∼𝒰⁡{0,…,K−1}t_{\nu}\!\sim\!\mathcal{U}\{0,\dots,K{-}1\} denote the diffusion timestep sampled independently for each frame ν\nu, following diffusion forcing (Chen et al., 2024a). With a noise schedule α¯t\bar{\alpha}_{t}, the per-frame forward corruption is

xtν(ν)=α¯tν​x0(ν)+1−α¯tν​ϵ(ν),ϵ(ν)∼𝒩⁡(0,I).x_{t_{\nu}}^{(\nu)}\;=\;\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t_{\nu}}}\;x_{0}^{(\nu)}\;+\;\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t_{\nu}}}\;\epsilon^{(\nu)},\quad\epsilon^{(\nu)}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I). (15)

Unlike the original ϵ\epsilon-parameterisation of Ho et al. (2020), the network directly predicts the clean signal x^0(ν)=Dϕ​(xtν(ν),tν,z)\hat{x}_{0}^{(\nu)}=D_{\phi}(x_{t_{\nu}}^{(\nu)},t_{\nu},z). The training loss sums per-frame x0x_{0}-MSE terms, with tνt_{\nu} promoted to a per-frame random variable inside the expectation:

ℒdec​(ϕ)=𝔼x0,{tν​∼iid​𝒰​{0,…,K−1}}ν,ϵ,z​[∑ν∥Dϕ​(xtν(ν),tν,z)−x0(ν)∥22].\mathcal{L}_{\text{dec}}(\phi)\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{x_{0},\;\{t_{\nu}\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}\mathcal{U}\{0,\ldots,K-1\}\}_{\nu},\;\epsilon,\;z}\!\left[\,\sum_{\nu}\big\lVert D_{\phi}(x_{t_{\nu}}^{(\nu)},t_{\nu},z)-x_{0}^{(\nu)}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}\,\right]. (16)

We use unweighted x0x_{0}-MSE, with no additional timestep-dependent weighting. For equivalent x0x_{0} and ϵ\epsilon predictions at 0<α¯t<10<\bar{\alpha}_{t}<1, the squared errors satisfy ‖x^0−x0‖2=1−α¯tα¯t​‖ϵ^−ϵ‖2\|\hat{x}_{0}-x_{0}\|^{2}=\frac{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\|\hat{\epsilon}-\epsilon\|^{2}. Thus, expressed as an ϵ\epsilon-prediction loss, this corresponds to inverse-SNR weighting, emphasizing high-noise rather than low-noise timesteps. The condition zz is dropped to the zero vector independently per sample with probability pdrop=0.1p_{\text{drop}}{=}0.1 during training to support classifier-free guidance (Ho and Salimans, 2022), although in practice we use a guidance scale of w=1.0w{=}1.0 (no guidance) by default since this is the most faithful for visualization. We use the log-SNR-parameterised cosine schedule of Simple Diffusion (Hoogeboom et al., 2023) in preference to the cosine schedule of IDDPM (Nichol and Dhariwal, 2021): parameterising in log-SNR gives finer control over the signal-to-noise trajectory and avoids the degenerate near-zero-SNR behavior at t→K−1t\!\to\!K{-}1 that the IDDPM schedule exhibits. We use K=1000K{=}1000 training timesteps and enforce zero terminal SNR following Lin et al. (2024); the per-frame independent tνt_{\nu}-sampling above is what makes the trained denoiser robust to mixed noise levels and, in turn, what enables prefix-conditioned generation at inference time.

Sampling.

Despite training with K=1000K{=}1000 DDPM steps, at inference we run only 2 DDIM steps (Song et al., 2021) from xK−1∼𝒩⁡(0,I)x_{K-1}\!\sim\!\mathcal{N}(0,I) per Cosmos frame and pipe the result through the frozen Cosmos decoder to pixels. We attribute this to the strength of the V-JEPA conditioning: dense V-JEPA 2.1 features already pin down most of the appearance, so the denoiser’s effective conditional distribution is nearly unimodal and its sampling path nearly straight. For streaming generation we keep the same local-window KV cache as the predictor (Appendix H) and write each new frame’s keys/values only on the last DDIM step so the cache never holds noisy activations; the streaming sampler runs at 44 DDIM steps per new frame, the small overhead buying robustness to the cache turnover. AOT compilation of DϕD_{\phi} for offline visualization is described alongside the predictor’s compilation pipeline in Appendix I; all decoder hyperparameters are collected in Table 11.
